summary: Describes use cases for measuring broadband performance across many homes and devices. Providers, users and regulators all have reasons to measure, and understanding these scenarios helped shape the LMAP framework. It is background material rather than a protocol.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 7536 describes two reasons to measure broadband performance at scale: a provider wants to know what its customers experience and where its network is at fault, and a regulator wants comparable numbers to publish and to check that providers treat traffic fairly. It then compares the ways to build the measurement system, and lists the security and privacy problems each brings.

subtitle: What large-scale measurements of broadband performance are for, and how the probes might be built.

tldr.problem: Providers and regulators both want to know how broadband actually performs, from the customer's home to the far end of the path, but measuring at scale raises cost, privacy and abuse questions.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 7536 sets out two use cases for large-scale measurement, what an operator and what a regulator want from it, and the ways a measurement system can be built, from dedicated hardware at the home gateway to an application on the user's own phone.
tldr.outcome: The document is a set of use cases that guide the framework, information model and protocols of the LMAP work. It closes with the security and privacy issues any such system has to answer, from probes being turned into attack platforms to the handling of personal data.

facts.label: Access technologies covered
facts.value: Fixed and mobile, over IPv4 and IPv6

today: RFC 7536 is an Informational RFC published in May 2015, and the unit metadata lists no document that obsoletes or updates it. It is a use cases document for the LMAP work, written to guide the framework, information model and protocol documents that came after it.

sections.title: Two Uses for Large-Scale Measurements
sections.content:
The document describes two use cases for the Large-scale Measurement of Broadband Performance, called LMAP. In the first, an internet service provider wants to understand the performance of its own network and the quality experienced by its customers. In the second, a regulator wants to provide information on the performance of the providers in its jurisdiction. Other use cases exist that are not the focus of the initial work, such as end users who want measurements to help identify a problem in their home network or to monitor their provider, and the same mechanisms are expected to apply to them.

From the point of view of the measurement work, there is no difference between a fixed service and a mobile one used for internet access, so measurements will be taken on both. Fixed services include DSL, cable and carrier Ethernet; mobile services include everything sold as 2G, 3G, 4G and Long Term Evolution. A metric defined to measure an end-to-end service will behave the same way on all access technologies, while other metrics may be specific to one. The architecture covers both IPv4 and IPv6 networks.
sections.plainLanguage: The document sets out who wants broadband performance measurements and why. A provider wants to know what its customers actually experience and where problems lie. A regulator wants numbers it can compare between providers and publish. Other groups, including customers themselves, are expected to use the same machinery later.

sections.title: The Internet Service Provider Use Case
sections.content:
A network operator needs to understand the performance of its own networks, of its suppliers both downstream and upstream, of its internet access services, and the effect of that performance on what customers experience. The processes it already runs, which are based on network measurement, include identifying, isolating and fixing problems, which may be in the operator's network, with the service provider, or in the customer's own equipment. Such problems may be common to a point in the topology, such as a single exchange, common to a vendor or equipment type such as a line card or home gateway, or unique to one user line such as copper access. Part of this work is helping users understand whether a problem is in their own home network or with a third-party application service rather than with the broadband product.

Design and planning is the second process. By monitoring the end-user experience, the operator can design and plan its network to keep the service at a specified level: services may be moved closer to users, upgraded, the effect of quality of service assessed, or more capacity deployed in particular places, and service level agreements may be defined at network or product boundaries. The third process is understanding the quality customers experience, which means the end-to-end view rather than the access portion alone, incorporating the home and enterprise networks and the effect of peering, caching and content delivery networks. The fourth is understanding the impact and operation of new devices and technology: as a new product is deployed or a new technology introduced, its operation and its impact have to be measured, which also quantifies what the new technology brings and supports the case for a wider rollout.
sections.plainLanguage: A provider runs four kinds of measurement work. It looks for faults, which often come from a shared point such as an exchange or from one kind of equipment rather than from one line. It plans the network by watching what customers experience. It tries to understand the whole path from the home to the far end, not just the access network. And it measures new products and technologies as it rolls them out, to show what they are worth.

sections.title: How an Operator Measures
sections.content:
The understanding of customer quality is gained through a panel of measurement probes deployed to several customers. A probe is a device or piece of software that makes measurements and reports the results under the control of the measurement system. The panel must include a representative sample of the operator's technologies and broadband speeds, for instance from below 8 Mbps to over 100 Mbps, and the operator wants the end-to-end view of the service rather than the access portion alone. That means relating the network parameters to something like a mean opinion score, which is service dependent, since web browsing quality is largely determined by latency once the speed is above a few Mbps. Compound metrics such as reliability may involve packet loss, DNS failures, retraining of the line and video streaming under-runs.

The operator really wants the end-to-end service experience, but the home network, whether Ethernet, Wi-Fi or powerline, is highly variable and outside its control. So far operators and regulators have measured from the home gateway instead, although a mobile operator clearly has to include the wireless link in the measurement. Active measurement is the most obvious approach, in which special measurement traffic is sent by and to the probe. To avoid degrading the service, that traffic should only be sent when the user is quiet, and it should not eat into the customer's data allowance. The alternative is passive measurement of the customer's ordinary traffic, which measures what the customer actually does but adds variability, because different traffic mixes give different results, and raises privacy concerns.

Several other operator tasks use the same machinery. New capabilities can be tested before rollout: whether a customer can be upgraded to a new broadband option, what the impact of IPv6 will be before it is offered, with questions such as whether IPv6 packets get through and what the latency to major websites will be, whether a new capability can be signalled using TCP options and how often a middlebox blocks it, and whether a quality of service mechanism works, for instance by checking that Differentiated Services markings are respected on a path. For planning, probing from several vantage points can show that a group of customers is below the expected performance at peak hours, which helps capacity planning, and there are parameters such as bufferbloat that equipment does not report and that are path metrics anyway. For service level agreements, the operator can spot the service degrading near the limit and be better informed when the contract is renewed, and can check the same for its suppliers, whether transit, content delivery networks, peering, a video source, or a local provider in a country where it has no network of its own. For faults, measurement gives a more nuanced view than alarms, since many issues are wide rather than point failures and so trigger too many alarms, while others degrade the service without triggering any at all. Measuring a subset of lines is enough to find problems that affect a group of customers, such as a shared exchange or a particular vendor, while measuring every line is what it takes to find problems unique to one customer. The operator also wants to narrow down whether a problem is in the home, in its own network, or with an application service, which means giving customers self-help tools, for example to reposition a device for better coverage, and giving the call centre the ability to run an on-demand test and get the result while the customer is still on the line.
sections.plainLanguage: The operator puts probes at a sample of customers, chosen to cover every technology and speed it sells, and reads the results as a picture of the whole service from the home to the far end. Active tests send special traffic, which has to wait until the customer is not using the line and must not use up their allowance. Passive tests watch the customer's own traffic, which is truer but noisier and raises privacy questions. The same measurements answer questions about new technology, about capacity at peak hours, about whether a service level agreement is about to be breached, and about where a fault lies.

sections.title: The Regulator Use Case
sections.content:
A regulator may want to evaluate the performance of the internet access services offered by operators. Each jurisdiction has its own concerns, but there is much in common: the need to produce datasets that compare providers, technical solutions, geographic and regional distributions, and the levels and combinations of broadband service that are marketed and provisioned. Regulators may publish performance measures as background information for end users, track the growth of high-speed broadband deployment, or monitor the traffic management practices of providers.

Because a regulator's role covers the development and enforcement of broadband policy, the measurement approach has to meet a high level of verifiability, accuracy and provider-independence, so that comparisons of service performance are valid and meaningful. The published information has to be accurate, meaning correct and not influenced by errors or side effects, and reproducible and consistent over time; comparable, meaning common metrics across providers, offerings and time; meaningful, meaning the metrics reflect what end users value about their service; and reliable, meaning the number and distribution of measurement agents and the statistical processing of the raw data are appropriate.

In practice, regulators measure from users towards several content and application providers, including dedicated test servers. Probes are distributed to a panel of selected end users covering all the operators and packages in the market, spread over urban, suburban and rural areas, and often including both fixed and mobile access. Periodic tests can measure actual speed at peak and off-peak hours and other quality metrics such as delay and jitter. The collected data then goes through statistical analysis, deriving estimates for the whole population, and summary information such as a service quality index is published regularly. Regulators may also let end users monitor their own service, to check it against their contract or to decide whether their subscription is the right one.

Measuring broadband deployment is the same activity done over time to see whether a country or region is improving against a strategic goal. Monitoring traffic management practices is the third area: a regulator may look for departures from application neutrality, such as blocking or throttling of particular applications, or preferential treatment of them, by sending or passively watching application-specific traffic and measuring in detail how the packets are carried. Detecting port blocking is relatively easy; detecting other kinds of differentiated treatment is a research topic in its own right, and the Glasnost paper and tool are an example of work in this area. A regulator may also compare the broadband service over time to see whether a specialised service is being provided at the expense of internet access, and compare providers or countries. The motivation is that regulatory approaches on net neutrality and the open internet have been introduced in some jurisdictions, and although legal challenges can change the status of a policy, the point for measurement is that policy-makers are looking for measurement solutions that help them find biased treatment of traffic flows.
sections.plainLanguage: A regulator publishes comparable numbers so that customers can choose between providers and so that the regulator can check what providers claim. The numbers have to be accurate, comparable between providers, meaningful to customers, and based on enough probes to be reliable. The same machinery shows whether broadband is improving over time, and whether a provider is treating some applications differently from others, which is what net neutrality rules are about.

sections.title: Ways to Build a Measurement System
sections.content:
One type of probe is a dedicated hardware device connected directly to the home gateway, deployed to a carefully selected panel of end users and running measurements on a defined schedule that can run throughout the day. Careful design ensures that measurements do not harm the user's experience and do not corrupt the results by testing while the user is on the line, so the system is tightly controlled by whoever runs it. The advantage is reliable benchmarks from only a few devices; the disadvantage is that deploying hardware at a scale fine enough to understand one broadband line would be expensive.

The other type puts the measurement capability in a webpage or application that end users are encouraged to download onto their phone or computer, with measurements triggered by the user, for example by pressing a button to test the broadband now. The performance is then measured to the end user rather than to the home gateway, so it includes the home network. The system is much more loosely controlled, because the panel and the schedule are set by the users rather than by the measurement system, which makes it easier to measure at a large scale but harder to get comparable benchmarks, since the results are affected by the home network, and because the population selects itself and may be biased towards those who think they have a problem. Encouraging wide use of the application and careful post-processing can reduce that bias. Other options are a variant on the first, with the measurement code built into the home gateway, which makes it viable on every line, and a variant on the second, where the user starts a measurement in response to a request from the measurement system.

Whoever runs the system has to make sure the measurements do not harm users. The traffic generated on a line may affect that user's quality of experience, and the danger is greater for measurements that generate a lot of traffic over a long period. The traffic may count against the user's bill or traffic cap. Traffic from several users may combine to congest a shared link. And the control and reporting traffic may overload the network, which is more likely where the traffic of many users is synchronised.
sections.plainLanguage: There are two main designs. Dedicated hardware at the gateway gives reliable, controlled results but costs money and does not scale to every line. An application on the user's own phone measures the whole path including the home network and scales cheaply, but the results vary with the user's own equipment and the people who volunteer are not a random sample. Whichever is used, the measurement traffic has to be kept from spoiling the user's service, their allowance, or a shared link.

sections.title: Security and Privacy Considerations
sections.content:
Large-scale measurement raises several security, privacy and business sensitivity issues. A malicious party may try to take control of probes to launch denial of service attacks, targeted at one user or group of users, at a network, or at a service provider. A malicious party may also take control of probes to create a platform for pervasive or targeted monitoring, for example by distributing a new measurement test that records and reports information of its own interest, and the same concerns arise if results are intercepted or corrupted.

Each party sees a different risk. For the end user, the concerns are a malicious party watching the traffic they send and receive, who they talk to, the sites they visit, and their behaviour and the location of their devices, and some of these are greater when the probe is on the user's own device rather than on the home gateway. For the network operator, the concerns are the leakage of commercially sensitive information about the design and operation of the network, its customers and its suppliers, including indirect ones such as an attacker reconnoitring weaknesses such as open ports and paths through the network. For the regulator, the concerns are distortion of the tests or alteration of the results, and a malicious operator identifying the lines being measured and prioritising that traffic.

There is also the matter of consent and of who is responsible. A measurement system that does not obtain the end user's informed consent, does not specify a particular purpose for it, or uses the information for secondary purposes is a problem. So is a system that does not make clear who is responsible for collecting and processing personal data and for fulfilling the rights of users. The responsible party, often called the data controller, should as good practice define the purpose for which the data is collected and used, how it is stored, accessed and processed, how long it is retained, and how an end user can view, update and even delete their personal data. If anonymised personal data is shared with a third party, the data controller should consider that the third party may be able to de-anonymise it by combining it with other information. These questions are considered further in the LMAP framework document, and the protocol documents that will instruct probes and collect their results will have to address them.
sections.plainLanguage: Running probes at people's homes creates real risks. Someone could take over a probe and use it to attack others or to watch what people do online. The operator risks leaking the design of its network, and the regulator risks results being distorted by an operator that knows which lines are being measured. On top of that, the people whose homes host the probes must agree to it, the purpose must be clear, and someone must be accountable for keeping the data and for letting people see and delete it.

viz.caption: THE TWO WAYS TO BUILD A MEASUREMENT PANEL

columns: Hardware probe at the home gateway
Application on the user's own device

cells: At the end user, so the home network is included
Varies with the home network, and the panel is self-selecting
Reliable benchmarks from a few devices, but expensive at scale
Cheap and easy to scale, but harder to get comparable numbers

viz.caption: WHAT PUBLISHED PERFORMANCE INFORMATION HAS TO BE

items.title: Accurate
items.text: The results must be correct, free of errors and side effects, and reproducible over time.

items.title: Comparable
items.text: The same metrics must be used across providers, offerings and time.

items.title: Meaningful
items.text: The metrics must reflect what end users value about their service.

items.title: Reliable
items.text: The number and spread of the agents, and the statistics applied to the data, must be right.

viz.caption: THE WAYS MEASUREMENT TRAFFIC CAN HARM A USER

items.title: Quality of experience
items.text: Long or heavy measurement traffic on the line affects what the user sees.

items.title: The bill or traffic cap
items.text: Measurement traffic counts against what the user has paid for.

items.title: A shared link
items.text: Traffic from several users can add up and congest a link they all use.

items.title: Synchronised reporting
items.text: Control and reporting traffic from many users at once can overload the network.
